description: For the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge, we are investigating the ocean's critical role in the carbon cycle. The ocean's capacity to absorb CO2 isn't uniform, it shifts regionally and temporally. We will leverage NASA satellite data to map out surface trends of ECCO-Darwin air-sea CO2 flux and Giovanni MERRA-2 Reanalysis sea surface temperature (SST), quantifying exactly where it is rising or falling, by how much, and evaluating the statistical significance of these changes.
summary:
By developing open-source Python code and Google Colab as a user-friendly framework, our team addressed the challenge by enabling the public to find any trend of Earth system as a detective. We used air-sea CO2 flux (FCO2) NASA ECCO-Darwin v5 dataset as an example. This creates an opportunity and benefits the general people who are interested in being an Earth system trend detective!
On average, the Niño 3.4 region is a main carbon dioxide (CO2) source of the Earth. We demonstrated the 21-year decadal trend of the air-sea CO2 flux (FCO2) in the Niño 3.4 region is positively increasing during boreal winter from 1998 to 2018 by up to 0.5 mol C⋅m−2⋅yr−1 per decade. Meanwhile, the temporal trends of MERRA-2 Reanalysis sea surface temperature and MODIS-Aqua chlorophyll-a downloaded from NASA Giovanni platform help explain the reasons of enhancing FCO2.
This framework aims to lower the threshold of the scientific mapping and finding trends from Earth’s data for anyone. We encourage users to explore the trend of any data they love when the spatial and temporal ranges change.
details:
The team C-Ocean chose the challenge called “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!.” By using Python code and Google Colab, our team built a user-friendly framework to enable the public to find any trend of Earth system as a detective, not only for our results (NASA ECCO-Darwin v5 dataset) but also for other standard data formats, such as HDF5 and netcdf for users. This creates an opportunity and benefits the people who are interested in being an Earth system trend detective! Details about how to conduct this project have been published on Github via this link: https://github.com/ja754969/Earth-data-detective-v6.git. 

The Niño 3.4 region is a key area in the central-to-east equatorial Pacific Ocean (PEQU-CE) bounded by 5°N–5°S and 170°W–120°W to serve as an index of El Niño–Southern Oscillation. On average, it is a main carbon dioxide (CO2) source of the Earth. Our team, C-Ocean, demonstrated the 21-year decadal trend of the air-sea CO2 flux (FCO2) in the Niño 3.4 region is positively increasing during boreal winter (December to February, DFJ) from 1998 to 2018 by up to 0.5 mol C⋅m−2⋅yr−1 per decade. Meanwhile, the annual trend of sea surface temperature (SST) in Niño 3.4 region is also positively increasing during DFJ from 1998 to 2018 by up to 0.2°C per year. The annual trend of chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) in Niño 3.4 region is also positively increasing during DFJ from 1998 to 2015 by up to 0.0014 mg⋅m−3 per year. The trends of SST and Chl-a explain the reasons of enhancing FCO2 in the Niño 3.4 region through thermal effect and non-thermal effect, respectively.

Based on the results in this presentation, we recommend that people who use this framework should be careful that different periods you choose can present different trends, driven by varying seasons and climate background (Tseng et al., 2026). This project aims to lower the threshold of the scientific mapping and finding trends from Earth’s data for anyone. We encourage users to explore the trend of any data they love when the spatial and temporal ranges change.
